problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(3{e}^{x}+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/785776cee4f82c5bfa5e86b5b1cb746b7c80f2d702fb52f67055a60bdff249ae.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3{e}^{x}+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3{e}^{x}+1.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3{e}^{x}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{x}+1.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3{e}^{x}+1.
$$
